Hoarsely means in a rough, raspy, and strained way — used to describe how someone speaks or makes a sound when their voice is not smooth or clear, but instead sounds scratchy, low, and forced, as if something is wrong with their throat.

Think of it this way: when a voice sounds normal, it is clear and flows easily. When someone speaks hoarsely, their voice sounds broken, gravelly, and a little painful — like it is being dragged across sandpaper.
What Does a Hoarse Voice Actually Sound Like?

To truly understand this word, you need a clear picture of the sound it describes.

Imagine:

  • A person who has been screaming at a concert for three hours straight — their voice the next morning, cracked and barely audible.
  • Someone who has had a bad cold or sore throat — their voice sounds rough, low, and scratchy when they try to speak.
  • A person who has been crying for a very long time — their voice gets thick, strained, and rough.
  • An old man who has smoked for decades — his voice might permanently sound gravelly and rough.

All of these voices share the same quality: they are not smooth. They sound like the throat is working too hard to produce sound. That quality — that rough, strained, scratchy sound — is what hoarse means, and hoarsely describes the manner in which someone speaks with that kind of voice.
How It Works as an Adverb

Since hoarsely is an adverb, it modifies a verb — it tells you how an action (usually speaking or making a sound) is being done.

Simple examples:

  • "Help me," she whispered hoarsely.
    → Her whisper was rough and scratchy, not smooth.
  • He spoke hoarsely after the surgery.
    → His speaking voice was strained and raspy.
  • She called out hoarsely for her dog in the rain.
    → She was calling out, but her voice sounded rough and worn.
  • "I can't do this anymore," he said hoarsely.
    → He said it in a cracked, strained voice — likely from exhaustion or emotion.
The Emotional Weight of This Word

This is an important layer. Writers and speakers don't just use hoarsely to describe a medical condition (like a sore throat). They use it to show emotion and effort as well. A hoarse voice is the natural result of the throat being pushed to its limits — either physically or emotionally.

So when you read "hoarsely" in a story or a sentence, it is almost always a signal of one or more of the following:

  • Exhaustion — the person has been talking, crying, or exerting themselves for too long.
  • Strong emotion — grief, fear, anger, desperation, or love can make the throat tighten, making the voice rough.
  • Urgency — the person is trying hard to speak even though their voice is failing them.
  • Illness — the person's throat is sore, dry, or infected.
  • Straining — the person has been shouting or yelling a lot.

For example:

  • "Please don't go," she begged hoarsely, tears running down her face.
    → You immediately feel her desperation and emotional pain — she has probably been crying, and her voice shows it.
  • "Run!" the soldier shouted hoarsely.
    → You sense he has been yelling warnings for a long time, and his voice is almost gone.

This emotional weight is what makes hoarsely such a powerful and expressive word. It doesn't just tell you what was said — it tells you what the person has been through.

It helps to know the full family this word belongs to:

  • Hoarse (adjective) — describes the voice itself. "His voice was hoarse." / "She had a hoarse cry."
  • Hoarsely (adverb) — describes how someone speaks or sounds. "She spoke hoarsely."
  • Hoarseness (noun) — refers to the condition or quality of being hoarse. "The hoarseness in his voice told her he had been crying."
How It Is Different from Similar Words

There are other words that describe rough or strained voices. Knowing the differences keeps your understanding sharp:

  • Huskily — A husky voice is also low and rough, but it often has a warm, attractive, or intimate quality to it. It doesn't necessarily imply strain or pain. A hoarse voice, on the other hand, suggests something is wrong — illness, exhaustion, or emotional distress. (Think: a singer might have a "husky" voice naturally, but a sick person would speak "hoarsely.")
  • Gruffly — This describes a voice that is rough and low because the person sounds unfriendly, stern, or blunt in manner. It's more about attitude than physical condition. A gruff person chooses to sound that way (or naturally does); a hoarse person cannot help it.
  • Raspily — Very close to hoarsely in meaning. Both describe a rough, scratchy voice. However, raspily focuses more on the specific scraping, rattling texture of the sound, while hoarsely is the broader and more commonly used term for the overall rough, strained quality.
A Quick Gut-Check to Always Remember

Whenever you read or hear the word hoarsely, ask yourself this: "Is this voice rough and strained because the throat has been pushed too far — by illness, emotion, or effort?"

If yes — that's hoarsely.

Picture a person who has just cried for an hour, or cheered at a stadium all night, or talked through a terrible fever. The voice they speak with after all of that — cracked, low, scratchy, barely holding together — is a hoarse voice. And when they use that voice to say something, they are speaking hoarsely.
